# Vibecoding Bootstrap — Hour 0 of EVERY hackathon build

> The standard scaffolding the coding agent must set up **before writing any feature code**. Goal: an automated, low-token, self-documenting vibecoding loop. **Every build playbook references this as its first build step.** Keep it lightweight — this is a hackathon, not production; simple hygiene only, no deep security.

---

## What gets created first (in order)

1. **`memory.md`** — the project's running brain (read first, updated last, every task).
2. **`AGENTS.md`** — the agent contract (how to work in this repo).
3. **`.github/copilot-instructions.md`** — same rules, for Copilot specifically (can be a one-line pointer to AGENTS.md).
4. **`README.md`** — what it is + how to run (stub now, grows as you build).
5. **`.env.example`** + **`.gitignore`** — never commit real secrets; `.env` is git-ignored.
6. **`scripts/`** (optional) — `setup.sh` / `run.sh` so the demo is reproducible in one command.
7. **`git init`** + first commit — Conventional Commits from the start.

## The memory.md protocol (the core of the automated loop)

`memory.md` is the single source of truth that keeps each prompt cheap and stateful.

**Rule for every prompt/task:**
1. **Read `memory.md` first** for context — do NOT re-scan the whole repo.
2. Do the task.
3. **Update `memory.md` last:** append what changed, decisions made, and next step. **Summarize aggressively** — bullet points, not transcripts. Prune stale detail. Keep it short to minimize token use next time.

Starter `memory.md`:

```markdown
# memory.md — <project> brain
> Read this first every task. Update it last. Keep it terse to save tokens.

## What this is
<one line>

## Stack
<languages/frameworks/services>

## Status snapshot
- Phase: <x>
- Last task: <what just shipped>
- Next: <immediate next step>

## Key decisions (why)
- <decision> — <reason>

## Open questions / TODO
- <item>

## File map (only what matters)
- `path` — purpose
```

## AGENTS.md (the contract the coding agent follows)

Keep it short. Include:

- **Loop rule:** "Read `memory.md` before each task; update it after. Summarize; don't dump."
- **Context discipline:** edit only relevant files; don't ingest the whole repo; prefer summaries.
- **Design rule:** "For any web UI, use the `frontend-design` skill." (See skills note below.)
- **Commits:** "After each working increment, commit with Conventional Commits." (format below)
- **Run discipline:** keep `README.md` run steps current; secrets only in `.env` (git-ignored).
- **Stop conditions:** ask before large refactors or adding heavy dependencies.

`.github/copilot-instructions.md` can simply say: *"Follow `AGENTS.md` in the repo root. Read `memory.md` first; update it last; keep context tight."*

## Skills: will they auto-fire?

Yes — heuristically. Copilot CLI auto-discovers `SKILL.md` skills from `~/.copilot/skills/`, `.github/skills/`, `.claude/skills/`, `.agents/skills/` and invokes one when the request matches its `description`. So **`frontend-design` fires automatically when you ask to build/style web UI** — but it's model judgment, not a guaranteed hook on a "UI phase." To make it reliable, **state it in `AGENTS.md`** ("use frontend-design for web UI") and/or name it in the prompt during the UI step.

> For hackathons, let it run with full creative freedom (bold, distinctive). If the project has an existing design system, add: "use frontend-design but conform to existing design tokens."

## Conventional Commits (auto, lightweight)

Format: `<type>(optional-scope): short summary`. Types you'll actually use:

| type | when |
|---|---|
| `feat` | new feature / capability |
| `fix` | bug fix |
| `docs` | README/markdown |

# Heads Up: Full A-to-Z Winning Playbook

> Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend · deadline **2026-10-05 06:59 UTC** · target publish **05:30 UTC**
> Categories: **Tinker · TabPFN · DigitalOcean · Entire · Sentry Agent Tracing** (+ Temporal, Copilot stretch) · overall prize.

> **⚠️ The friend must be real.** The rules require "a real problem for a friend or loved one", and the post's power comes from a real reaction. Every `[BRACKET]` below gets filled with real data. **Never invent a metric, a quote, or a person.** If your friend doesn't get migraines, use the swap table in §1.5. The architecture stays identical.

## TABLE OF CONTENTS
I. Strategy · II. Build (hour-by-hour) · III. Persuasion · IV. Full draft post · V. Promotion · VI. Submission checklist

---

# PART I — STRATEGY & POSITIONING

## 1.1 The thesis (memorize this)
**"I can't fix [Friend]'s head, but I can give them a forecast. A tiny open model I fine-tuned reads their messy texts, a tabular foundation model reads their history, and it all runs on one box I control, so their health notes never touch anyone else's API."**

## 1.2 Judging criteria → design choices

| Criterion | Design choice that scores it |
|---|---|
| **Writing (weighted most)** | Real friend, real first scene, a results table with honest caveats, a "[Friend] said / what I changed" table (copy the BMW entry's best move), 6–9 min read. |
| Relevance (open AI at the core) | Two open models are the product: a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B (weights downloaded, self-hosted) + local TabPFN-3.5. Remove either and nothing works. |
| Creativity | Migraine forecasting: 0 of 786 entries. A "weather forecast for your head" framing. The Shapley "why" turns a probability into advice. |
| Technical execution | Live URL + repo + 90-second video. Eval scripts in the repo reproduce every number. Sentry traces prove it runs. |
| Partner tech | Each of the 5 is load-bearing (see §2.1). The post has one subsection per category with a screenshot or number. |

## 1.3 Persona (who reads it)
A DEV judge reading 900 entries in a week. They've seen 265 "local Gemma companion" posts. They reward: **a person, a number, a working link, honesty.** They punish: a stack list without a reason, invented stats, and dead demos.

## 1.4 Cut list (do NOT build)
- ❌ Accounts/auth. One passphrase-protected private profile + a public demo profile.
- ❌ Mobile app. A responsive web page they can "Add to Home Screen".
- ❌ Voice input. A cloud voice API contradicts the privacy thesis, and local Whisper costs an hour.
- ❌ Gemma, Render, ElevenLabs, a vector DB (see `02`).
- ❌ Push notifications (unless Temporal stretch). The page shows tomorrow's forecast. The friend checks it at night.

## 1.5 Friend swap table (same code, different nouns)

| Friend's situation | Notes they write | Row fields (Tinker parses) | TabPFN target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Migraines (default)** | "5h sleep, 3 coffees, excel till 9, neck tight" | sleep_h, caffeine, screen_h, stress 1–5, skipped_meal, neck, aura, alcohol, cycle_day? | migraine_next_day (0/1) |
| Eczema/asthma flare | "dusty office, new detergent, itchy at night" | exposures, sleep, stress, products | flare_next_day |
| Runner with niggles | "8k easy, left calf tight, bad sleep" | km, pace, rpe, soreness_site, sleep | pain_next_run |
| Café owner | WhatsApp orders: "2 sourdough + 6 croissant for sat pls" | item, qty, pickup_day | units_sold tomorrow (regression) |

---

# PART II — BUILD PHASE

## 2.0 Pre-flight (first 20 min, in parallel, before code)
1. **Message the friend NOW** (they may be asleep later). Ask for: (a) their last 60–120 days of anything: notes app, texts to you, a tracker export, painkiller purchase dates, calendar; (b) which days they had a migraine (rough is fine); (c) their city (for weather); (d) 20 typical "how was today" texts in their own words; (e) consent to describe them in a public post (first name or a nickname).
2. **Claim credits:** https://hacktoberfest.com/my/promos → Tinker (required), plus any DigitalOcean credit available. Create keys: Tinker (`TINKER_API_KEY`), Prior Labs (`TABPFN_TOKEN`, used only for weight download/auth), Sentry project (Python, `SENTRY_DSN`), DO API token (`doctl auth init`).
3. **Hour-1 go/no-go gates** (run each in under 5 min; record ✅/✗ for the post's capability grid):
   - `python -c "import tinker; print(tinker.ServiceClient().get_server_capabilities())"` → Tinker auth works.
   - `pip install tabpfn && python -c "from tabpfn import TabPFNClassifier; TabPFNClassifier().fit([[0],[1]]*5,[0,1]*5)"` → local weights download (may require accepting the license / HF auth. See [Accessing Model Weights](https://docs.priorlabs.ai/models/accessing-model-weights.md)).
   - `doctl compute size list | grep s-4vcpu-8gb` → DO account can create the Droplet.

## 2.1 Stack (and each piece's job)

| Layer | Choice | Why this, not the alternative |
|---|---|---|
| Parser model | **Qwen3.5-4B + LoRA, trained on Tinker** (`Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B`, $0.737/M train tokens) | 4B Q4 fits in about 3 GB and runs on a CPU Droplet. The 9B is more accurate zero-shot but roughly 2× slower on CPU. The fine-tune closes that gap, and that's the Tinker proof. |
| Teacher (dataset labels only) | A large open model sampled on Tinker (e.g. `Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B` or `moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6`) | It's open too, so the whole pipeline is open weights end to end. Used **offline** on synthetic notes only, never on the friend's real notes. |
| Forecaster | **TabPFN-3.5, local `tabpfn` package** + `tabpfn-extensions[interpretability]` | Base TabPFN-3.5 runs locally, so health rows stay on the box. Plus/Thinking are API-only, and that's exactly why we don't use them. Raw DataFrame in, no encoding needed. |
| Serving | **llama.cpp → GGUF Q4_K_M via Ollama** on the Droplet (OpenAI-compatible `:11434/v1`) | The same OpenAI client works against Tinker (eval) and Ollama (prod), and Sentry's OpenAI integration traces both. |
| App | FastAPI + one HTML page (frontend-design skill) + SQLite | Smallest thing that works. SQLite lives on the Droplet: no third-party DB. |
| Host | **DigitalOcean Droplet** `s-4vcpu-8gb`, Ubuntu 24.04, Caddy + `<ip>.sslip.io` for HTTPS | Self-hosting the *fine-tuned* model is the unclaimed DO story. (Serverless Inference can't serve your own LoRA.) |
| Tracing | **Sentry** Python SDK + `OpenAIIntegration(include_prompts=False)` + manual agent/tool spans | `include_prompts=False` keeps health text out of Sentry: the same privacy line, applied to observability. |
| Build provenance | **Entire** (`entire enable -y --agent claude-code`) | Every Claude Code session becomes a checkpoint tied to a commit. Link 3–4 key ones in the post. |
| Weather | Open-Meteo historical + forecast API (free, no key) | Pressure change is a widely reported migraine trigger. It gives TabPFN a feature the friend doesn't have to log. |

## 2.2 Hour-by-hour (H0 = when you start; ~9h build)

### H0:00–0:30 — Bootstrap (vibecoding flow, always first)
Per `tracks/hackathon-research/vibecoding-bootstrap.md`:
```bash
mkdir heads-up && cd heads-up && git init
entire enable -y --agent claude-code      # BEFORE the first agent session, so every session is captured
# create: memory.md, AGENTS.md (loop rule, "use frontend-design for UI", Conventional Commits),
#         .github/copilot-instructions.md, README.md, .env.example, .gitignore (.env, data/private/, *.gguf), LICENSE (MIT)
git add -A && git commit -m "chore: bootstrap heads-up"
gh repo create heads-up --public --source . --push
```

**Tinker SFT (`train/sft.py`)** (from the [quickstart](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/tinker/quickstart/index.md)):
```python
import json, random, tinker
SYSTEM = "Extract a JSON row with keys: sleep_h, caffeine_cups, screen_h, stress, skipped_meal, alcohol_units, neck_tension, aura, exercise_min, notes_other. Output JSON only."
sc = tinker.ServiceClient()
tc = sc.create_lora_training_client(base_model="Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B", rank=32)
tok = tc.get_tokenizer()

def datum(note, row):
    prompt = tok.apply_chat_template([{"role":"system","content":SYSTEM},{"role":"user","content":note}],
                                     add_generation_prompt=True)          # verify: renderer for Qwen3.5 (disable thinking)
    completion = tok.encode(json.dumps(row) + tok.eos_token, add_special_tokens=False)
    full = prompt + completion
    return tinker.types.Datum(
        model_input=tinker.types.ModelInput.from_ints(full[:-1]),         # verify field name: input vs model_input
        loss_fn_inputs={"target_tokens": full[1:],
                        "weights": [0.0]*(len(prompt)-1) + [1.0]*len(completion)})

data = [json.loads(l) for l in open("data/train.jsonl")]
for epoch in range(3):
    random.shuffle(data)
    for i in range(0, len(data), 16):
        batch = [datum(d["note"], d["row"]) for d in data[i:i+16]]
        fb = tc.forward_backward(batch, loss_fn="cross_entropy")
        tc.optim_step(tinker.types.AdamParams(learning_rate=2e-4)).result()
        print(epoch, i, fb.result().metrics)                               # log loss for the post's curve
path = tc.save_weights_for_sampler(name="heads-up-v1").result().path        # verify; -> tinker://... sampler path
print(path)
```

**Forecast + why (`app/forecast.py`):**
```python
import pandas as pd
from tabpfn import TabPFNClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import RepeatedStratifiedKFold, cross_val_score

def train_eval(hist: pd.DataFrame):
    X, y = hist.drop(columns=["date","migraine_next_day"]), hist["migraine_next_day"]
    cv = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=5, random_state=0)
    auc = cross_val_score(TabPFNClassifier(), X, y, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")
    return auc.mean(), auc.std()

def forecast(hist, today_row):
    clf = TabPFNClassifier().fit(hist.drop(columns=["date","migraine_next_day"]), hist["migraine_next_day"])
    p = clf.predict_proba(today_row)[0, 1]
    # Shapley drivers: tabpfn-extensions interpretability (shapiq) -> top-3 features by |value|  # verify API in docs
    return p
```

**Why you need a real person at all:**
1. **It's in the rules.** The entry has to "solve a real problem for a friend or loved one." A made-up person risks disqualification and reads as fake.

- **Gym or sport:** "chest day, bench felt heavy, slept 6h" → will he hit a personal best or get sore tomorrow?
- **Studies or exams:** daily study notes → which topics he's likely to fail on the next test
- **Sleep, skin breakouts, allergies or stomach issues:** daily log → chance of a bad day tomorrow
- **Money:** spending texts → will he run out before the end of the month?

- 20 or more examples of how he'd describe his day, in his own words and slang

# Actually: Playbook (ADHD / time-blindness edition)

> **Supersedes the *domain* parts of `03-PLAYBOOK-heads-up.md`** (data, schema, eval, post). Infrastructure is unchanged and still lives there: bootstrap §H0, Tinker SFT skeleton §2.3, GGUF export + DigitalOcean §H4:30, Sentry §H5:30, Entire, submission checklist Part VI. The stack is the same five: **Tinker · TabPFN · DigitalOcean · Sentry · Entire**.
> **Deadline: Mon Oct 5, 11:59 AM PKT (06:59 UTC). Publish by 10:30 AM PKT.**

## 1. The idea in one breath
Your friend has ADHD. One of the most-reported ADHD struggles is **time blindness**: "this'll take 15 minutes" becomes an hour, the day is over-packed by 9 AM, and the guilt follows. **Actually** takes his messy brain-dump (*"email prof abt extension, laundry maybe, gym, finish dbms assignment, call ammi back"*). A **Tinker-fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B** splits it into structured tasks. Then **TabPFN**, reading *his own* history of guessed vs real durations, tells him **how long each task will actually take *him***, with a range and a reason, and what really fits in the hours he has.

> *"You think this list is 2h10m. For you, it's about 4h40m (3h50–5h30). You've got 3 free hours. Do these three; the laundry and the email can move to tomorrow — you finish admin tasks after 9 PM only 20% of the time."*

**Why this wins:**
- **Not taken.** 8 ADHD/overwhelm entries exist, all with ≤3♥, and all of them are "LLM breaks your task into steps" chat apps (Unstick, Kaizen, BiteSize, Promise Keeper…). **0 of 786 entries tackle time blindness or duration prediction.**
- **TabPFN is the textbook fit, and it gives the most intuitive metric in the contest:** *"TabPFN's estimates of how long his tasks take are [X]% closer to reality than his own guesses."* Every reader, ADHD or not, gets it in one line. It's in-context too: every task he logs makes the next prediction better instantly, with no retraining (a genuine TabPFN-only property worth stating).
- **Tinker has a hard, real job.** Rambling multi-task brain-dumps ("maybe", "after that", Urdu/English mix, slang) are where small base models drop or merge tasks. Measure task-level F1 on *his real* dumps.
- **Open-innovation story is strong.** An ADHD diagnosis, meds, and daily struggles are health data. Everything runs on one Droplet you control, and Sentry traces exclude prompts.

## 2. What to get from your friend TONIGHT (15–20 min; send this message now)

> "Building you something for the hackathon, need 15 min of your help before you sleep:
> 1. Paste me 5–10 brain-dumps / to-do rants you've actually written or sent me (notes app, WhatsApp, anything). Plus write 3 fresh ones right now about tomorrow.
> 2. Fill this sheet with as many tasks as you can remember from the last 2–3 weeks (aim for 40+): what it was, how long you THOUGHT it would take, how long it ACTUALLY took (rough is fine), did it get done the day you planned (y/n), what time you started.
> 3. Is it ok if I write about you in a public post (first name or nickname)?
> 4. Tomorrow morning: try it for 5 minutes and tell me honestly what's wrong with it."

**Sheet columns** (Google Sheet → CSV): `date, task, kind, guess_min, actual_min, done_same_day, start_hour, dreaded(y/n), left_house(y/n)` + optional `slept_h, meds_taken(y/n)`. Kind = admin · study · creative · chore · errand · social · work.

Sources that jog memory: WhatsApp chats with you ("bro still haven't done X"), Google Calendar, uni portal submission timestamps vs deadlines, phone screen-time.
**Honest caveat for the post:** remembered durations are noisy. Say so, then add a small set of *live* logged rows from tomorrow morning if possible.

## 3. Schemas (fix now, never change)

**Tinker parser output** (brain-dump → tasks):
```json
{"tasks": [
  {"title": "email prof about extension", "kind": "admin", "guess_min": null,
   "deadline": "today", "must_leave_house": false, "dreaded": true, "depends_on": null},
  {"title": "laundry", "kind": "chore", "guess_min": 30, "deadline": null,
   "must_leave_house": false, "dreaded": false, "depends_on": null, "optional": true}
]}
```

**TabPFN table** (one row per past task): features `kind, guess_min, start_hour, day_of_week, dreaded, left_house, deadline_hours, [slept_h], [meds_taken]` → targets
- `actual_min`: **TabPFNRegressor** with its predictive distribution → median + 10–90% range ([Predictive Distribution](https://docs.priorlabs.ai/capabilities/predictive-distribution.md))
- `done_same_day`: **TabPFNClassifier** → P(finished today)
- Shapley drivers via `tabpfn-extensions[interpretability]` → "because: admin + after 9 PM + dreaded"

## 4. Eval (these numbers ARE the post)

**TabPFN (the headline):** cross-validated on his rows (repeated 5-fold).

| Estimator of actual duration | MAE (min) | within ±25% |
|---|---|---|
| His own guess | [ ] | [ ]% |
| "Multiply by 2" rule of thumb | [ ] | [ ]% |
| His guess × his median overrun ratio | [ ] | [ ]% |
| Linear regression | [ ] | [ ]% |
| **TabPFN** | **[ ]** | **[ ]%** |

Including the two "dumb" baselines is what makes the result credible. If TabPFN only narrowly beats "his ratio", say so. That is still a finding.

**Tinker:** parser on **his real brain-dumps, hand-labelled** (10–15 dumps ≈ 60–100 tasks).

| Parser | valid JSON | task F1 (found the right tasks) | kind acc | guess_min acc | p50 latency on Droplet |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.5-4B zero-shot | | | | | |
| Qwen3.5-4B 5-shot | | | | | |
| Qwen3.5-9B zero-shot | | | | | |
| **Qwen3.5-4B + LoRA** | | | | | |

Plus the downstream column: **error in the total-day forecast** when the plan is built from each parser's output. Dropped or merged tasks make the day look shorter than it is, which is exactly the time-blindness bug the app exists to fix. That's a great line for the post.

**Training data:** about 400 synthetic brain-dumps written by a large open teacher on Tinker (e.g. `Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B`), seeded with the *style* of 5 of his real dumps (keep the rest as the test set), labelled by the teacher, and spot-checked by you. Cost is under $1.

## 5. Hour plan (PKT, starting ~00:15)

| PKT | Do |
|---|---|
| 00:15–00:45 | Send the friend message. Bootstrap the repo + `entire enable -y --agent claude-code`. Claim Tinker credits. Go/no-go gates (Tinker auth, local `tabpfn` weights, `doctl`). |
| 00:45–02:15 | Synthetic dataset → **start the Tinker SFT run** (it trains while you build). Meanwhile: TabPFN module on his sheet + CV eval table. |
| 02:15–04:00 | FastAPI + one-page UI (frontend-design): brain-dump box → task cards with "you: 15m · actually: 45m (30–70)" → "fits in your free time" plan → one-tap "done + how long". |
| 04:00–05:00 | Parser eval (base vs tuned) → fill table. Export adapter → GGUF → Ollama. |
| 05:00–06:00 | DigitalOcean Droplet up, HTTPS via sslip.io, demo profile with synthetic data, private profile with a passphrase. |
| 06:00–06:30 | Sentry traces (base vs tuned latency, one bug found) → screenshots. |
| **06:30–08:00** | **Sleep 90 min** (an alarm-proof one). |
| 08:00–08:30 | Friend tries it. Get their verbatim reaction, make one fix. |
| 08:30–10:15 | Write the post (structure §6), cover image, 60–90 s video. |
| **10:15–10:30** | Checklist (Part VI of heads-up playbook) → **PUBLISH**. Then MLH Discord + socials. |
| 11:59 | Deadline. |

**Cut order if behind:** (1) Sentry → (2) GGUF self-hosting (use the Tinker OpenAI endpoint; DO still hosts the app) → (3) the downstream parser column. **Never cut:** the TabPFN-vs-his-guesses table, the friend's quote, the live link.

## 6. Post outline (template headings, exact)

Title candidates:
1. *"My friend thinks everything takes 15 minutes. I built him a model that knows better."*
2. *"Time blindness, measured: TabPFN guesses my ADHD friend's tasks [X]% better than he does"*

- **Opening:** "[Friend] has ADHD. Ask him how long an email takes and he'll say five minutes. Last [Tuesday] it took [real story]." + the honest "I can't fix time blindness, but I can show him the number."
- **What I Built:** brain-dump in → real durations + a day that actually fits. Screenshot.
- **Demo:** live link (demo profile) + video.
- **Code:** repo embed, MIT, `eval/` reproduces every number.
- **How I Built It:** (1) Tinker parser + table; (2) TabPFN + the his-guess-vs-TabPFN table + Shapley "why"; (3) one DigitalOcean Droplet; (4) Sentry traces + the bug; capability grid with honest ✗s.
- **Why Does Open Innovation Matter?:** health data on his box; a model fine-tuned to *his* ramble that you can't get from a closed API; runs for ~nothing and outlives the hackathon. Plus one line where closed would have been better.
- **What [Friend] said:** verbatim quote + "He said / What I changed" table.
- **My Agent Session:** Entire checkpoint links (3–4 key decisions) (+ optional DevRelay).
- **Prize Categories:** Tinker · TabPFN · DigitalOcean · Sentry Agent Tracing · Entire, one line of proof each.
- **Closing question:** "If you have ADHD: what's the task you're *always* wrong about?"

**Sensitivity rule:** describe ADHD the way your friend describes it, and let him read the post before you publish. No medical claims. It's "a planning aid", not treatment.

from typing import Literal, Optional

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

Kind = Literal["admin", "study", "creative", "chore", "errand", "social", "work", "health"]


class Task(BaseModel):
    title: str
    kind: Kind = "admin"
    guess_min: Optional[int] = None
    deadline: Optional[Literal["today", "tomorrow", "this_week"]] = None
    must_leave_house: bool = False
    dreaded: bool = False
    optional: bool = False


class TaskList(BaseModel):
    tasks: list[Task] = Field(default_factory=list)


class Forecast(BaseModel):
    title: str
    kind: str
    guess_min: Optional[int]

"""TabPFN on the friend's own task history.

Regressor: how long a task will actually take him (median + 10-90% range).
Classifier: probability he finishes it the day he planned it.
Both are in-context: every logged task improves the next prediction with no retraining.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
import math

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

FEATURES = ["kind", "guess_min", "start_hour", "day_of_week", "dreaded", "left_house", "has_deadline"]
MIN_ROWS = 12


def load_history(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
    df.columns = [c.strip().lower() for c in df.columns]
    for c in ("dreaded", "left_house", "done_same_day"):
        if c in df:
            df[c] = df[c].astype(str).str.strip().str.lower().isin(["y", "yes", "1", "true"]).astype(int)
    if "date" in df:
        df["day_of_week"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"], errors="coerce").dt.dayofweek
    df["has_deadline"] = df.get("has_deadline", 0)
    df = df[pd.to_numeric(df["actual_min"], errors="coerce").notna()].copy()
    df["actual_min"] = df["actual_min"].astype(float)
    df["guess_min"] = pd.to_numeric(df["guess_min"], errors="coerce")
    return df


def task_rows(tasks, now: dt.datetime | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    now = now or dt.datetime.now()
    return pd.DataFrame([{
        "kind": t.kind,
        "guess_min": t.guess_min if t.guess_min is not None else np.nan,
        "start_hour": now.hour,
        "day_of_week": now.weekday(),
        "dreaded": int(t.dreaded),
        "left_house": int(t.must_leave_house),
        "has_deadline": int(t.deadline is not None),
    } for t in tasks])


class Forecaster:
    def __init__(self, history: pd.DataFrame):
        from tabpfn import TabPFNClassifier, TabPFNRegressor

        self.history = history
        X = history[FEATURES]
        # log-duration: durations are right-skewed; TabPFN is happier on the log scale
        self.reg = TabPFNRegressor().fit(X, np.log1p(history["actual_min"]))
        self.clf = None
        y = history.get("done_same_day")
        if y is not None and y.nunique() == 2:
            self.clf = TabPFNClassifier().fit(X, y)
        self.overrun = float(np.nanmedian(history["actual_min"] / history["guess_min"]))

    def predict(self, rows: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
        q = self.reg.predict(rows[FEATURES], output_type="quantiles", quantiles=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
        p10, p50, p90 = (np.expm1(np.asarray(a)) for a in q)
        p_done = self.clf.predict_proba(rows[FEATURES])[:, 1] if self.clf is not None else [None] * len(rows)
        return {"p10": p10, "p50": p50, "p90": p90, "p_done": p_done}

    def why(self, row: pd.Series) -> list[str]:
        """Plain-English drivers from the friend's own history (cheap, deterministic).
        Shapley attributions (tabpfn-extensions) are computed offline in eval/ for the post."""
        h, out = self.history, []
        same = h[h["kind"] == row["kind"]]
        if len(same) >= 3 and same["guess_min"].notna().any():
            r = float(np.nanmedian(same["actual_min"] / same["guess_min"]))
            if math.isfinite(r) and r > 1.2:
                out.append(f"{row['kind']} tasks take you ~{r:.1f}x your guess")
        if row["dreaded"] and h["dreaded"].sum() >= 3:
            d = h.groupby("dreaded")["actual_min"].median()
            if 1 in d and 0 in d and d[1] > d[0]:
                out.append(f"dreaded tasks run ~{d[1] / d[0]:.1f}x longer for you")
        late = h[h["start_hour"] >= 21]
        if row["start_hour"] >= 21 and len(late) >= 3 and "done_same_day" in h:
            out.append(f"you finish only {late['done_same_day'].mean():.0%} of tasks started after 9 PM")
        return out[:3]

"""SQLite on the host box: logged tasks become new TabPFN context rows."""
import os
import sqlite3

DB_PATH = os.getenv("DB_PATH", "actually.db")


def conn():
    c = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    c.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS logged (
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, profile TEXT, date TEXT, task TEXT, kind TEXT, guess_min REAL,
        actual_min REAL, done_same_day INTEGER, start_hour INTEGER, dreaded INTEGER, left_house INTEGER,
        has_deadline INTEGER)""")
    return c


def log_task(profile: str, row: dict):
    with conn() as c:
        c.execute("""INSERT INTO logged (profile,date,task,kind,guess_min,actual_min,done_same_day,start_hour,
                     dreaded,left_house,has_deadline) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)""",
                  (profile, row["date"], row["task"], row["kind"], row.get("guess_min"), row["actual_min"],
                   row.get("done_same_day", 1), row["start_hour"], row.get("dreaded", 0),
                   row.get("left_house", 0), row.get("has_deadline", 0)))


def logged_rows(profile: str):
    import pandas as pd

    with conn() as c:
        return pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM logged WHERE profile = ?", c, params=(profile,))

"""Sentry Agent Tracing. Prompts are never sent: the friend's brain-dumps stay on the box."""
import contextlib
import os

import sentry_sdk


def init():
    dsn = os.getenv("SENTRY_DSN")
    if not dsn:
        return
    from sentry_sdk.integrations.openai import OpenAIIntegration

    sentry_sdk.init(

@contextlib.contextmanager

@contextlib.contextmanager

}

OVERRUN = {"admin": 2.6, "study": 1.7, "chore": 1.3, "errand": 1.5, "social": 1.8, "creative": 2.0, "work": 1.9,

"""Synthetic training data for the parser, made by a large OPEN teacher model on Tinker.

1. The teacher writes brain-dumps in the friend's style (style seeds = a few of his real dumps,
   never the held-out test dumps).
2. The teacher labels each dump with the exact schema in app/prompts.py.
Output: data/synthetic/train.jsonl  ({"note": str, "gold": {"tasks": [...]}})

Usage: python -m train.gen_synthetic --n 400 --seeds data/private/style_seeds.txt
"""
import argparse
import json
import random
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

import tinker
from dotenv import load_dotenv

from app.parser import TinkerParser, render_prompt

load_dotenv()
TEACHER = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B"

SCENARIOS = [
    "a uni student the night before a deadline", "a lazy sunday with chores piling up",
    "a monday with classes, gym and family calls", "a day full of admin they keep avoiding",
    "a freelance + study day", "exam week panic", "after a bad night's sleep", "a day with errands across town",
    "a weekend with a wedding to attend", "a guilt-heavy day after skipping yesterday's plans",
]
WRITE_PROMPT = """Write ONE realistic, messy brain-dump (a to-do rant) by a young person in Pakistan with ADHD, for: {scenario}.
Style rules: write like these real examples (casual, run-on, lowercase, some Urdu/English mix, "maybe", "ugh", tangents):
{seeds}
Mention {k} distinct tasks. Sometimes state a duration ("should take 20 min"), sometimes not. Output only the brain-dump text."""


def write_dump(sampler, tok, seeds: list[str]) -> str:
    seed_txt = "\n---\n".join(random.sample(seeds, min(3, len(seeds))))
    msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": WRITE_PROMPT.format(scenario=random.choice(SCENARIOS), seeds=seed_txt,
                                                           k=random.randint(2, 8))}]
    res = sampler.sample(prompt=tinker.types.ModelInput.from_ints(render_prompt(tok, msgs)), num_samples=1,
                         sampling_params=tinker.types.SamplingParams(max_tokens=400, temperature=0.9)).result()
    return tok.decode(res.sequences[0].tokens, skip_special_tokens=True).strip()


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=400)
    ap.add_argument("--seeds", default="data/private/style_seeds.txt")
    ap.add_argument("--out", default="data/synthetic/train.jsonl")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    seeds = [s.strip() for s in Path(a.seeds).read_text().split("---") if s.strip()]
    sampler = tinker.ServiceClient().create_sampling_client(base_model=TEACHER)
    tok = sampler.get_tokenizer()
    labeler = TinkerParser(TEACHER)

    def one(_):
        dump = write_dump(sampler, tok, seeds)
        r = labeler.parse(dump)
        return {"note": dump, "gold": r.tasks.model_dump()} if r.tasks and r.tasks.tasks else None

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(16) as ex:
        rows = [r for r in ex.map(one, range(a.n)) if r]
    Path(a.out).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with open(a.out, "w") as f:
        for r in rows:
            f.write(json.dumps(r, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    print(f"wrote {len(rows)}/{a.n} -> {a.out}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""LoRA SFT of Qwen3.5-4B on Tinker. Loss only on the assistant JSON tokens.

Usage: python -m train.sft --data data/synthetic/train.jsonl --epochs 3
Prints the sampler path (tinker://...) to put in .env as TINKER_SAMPLER_PATH.
"""
import argparse
import json
import random

import tinker
from dotenv import load_dotenv

from app.parser import messages, render_prompt

load_dotenv()
BASE = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B"


def make_datum(tok, note: str, gold: dict) -> tinker.types.Datum:
    prompt = render_prompt(tok, messages(note))
    completion = tok.encode(json.dumps(gold, ensure_ascii=False) + "<|im_end|>", add_special_tokens=False)
    full = prompt + completion
    weights = [0.0] * (len(prompt) - 1) + [1.0] * len(completion)
    return tinker.types.Datum(
        model_input=tinker.types.ModelInput.from_ints(full[:-1]),
        loss_fn_inputs={"target_tokens": full[1:], "weights": weights},
    )


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--data", default="data/synthetic/train.jsonl")
    ap.add_argument("--epochs", type=int, default=3)
    ap.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=16)
    ap.add_argument("--lr", type=float, default=2e-4)
    ap.add_argument("--rank", type=int, default=32)
    ap.add_argument("--name", default="actually-v1")
    a = ap.parse_args()

    rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open(a.data)]
    tc = tinker.ServiceClient().create_lora_training_client(base_model=BASE, rank=a.rank)
    tok = tc.get_tokenizer()
    data = [make_datum(tok, r["note"], r["gold"]) for r in rows]
    steps = a.epochs * ((len(data) + a.batch - 1) // a.batch)
    step, log = 0, open("results/train_log.jsonl", "w")
    for epoch in range(a.epochs):
        random.shuffle(data)
        for i in range(0, len(data), a.batch):
            lr = a.lr * (1 - step / steps)  # linear decay
            fb = tc.forward_backward(data[i:i + a.batch], loss_fn="cross_entropy")
            tc.optim_step(adam_params=tinker.types.AdamParams(learning_rate=lr)).result()
            out = fb.result()
            metrics = getattr(out, "metrics", {}) or {}
            log.write(json.dumps({"step": step, "epoch": epoch, "lr": lr, **metrics}) + "\n")
            log.flush()
            print(step, epoch, {k: round(v, 4) if isinstance(v, float) else v for k, v in metrics.items()})
            step += 1
    path = tc.save_weights_for_sampler(name=a.name).result().path
    print("SAMPLER_PATH", path)
    with open("results/sampler_path.txt", "w") as f:
        f.write(path + "\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Headline eval: does TabPFN predict how long his tasks take better than he does?

Repeated K-fold CV on the task history. Baselines: his own guess, "x2" rule, his-median-overrun x guess,
linear regression. Usage: python -m eval.tabpfn_eval --csv data/private/tasks.csv --label friend
"""
import argparse
import json

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import RepeatedKFold
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

from app.forecast import FEATURES, load_history


def metrics(y, p):
    y, p = np.asarray(y), np.asarray(p)
    return {"mae_min": float(np.mean(np.abs(y - p))), "within_25pct": float(np.mean(np.abs(p - y) <= 0.25 * y))}


def main():
    from tabpfn import TabPFNRegressor

    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--csv", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--label", default="demo")
    ap.add_argument("--repeats", type=int, default=3)
    a = ap.parse_args()
    df = load_history(a.csv)
    df = df[df["guess_min"].notna()].reset_index(drop=True)
    X, y = df[FEATURES], df["actual_min"].values
    preds = {k: np.zeros((a.repeats, len(df))) for k in ["his_guess", "x2_rule", "his_overrun", "linear", "tabpfn"]}
    lin = make_pipeline(
        ColumnTransformer([("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["kind"])], remainder="passthrough"),
        SimpleImputer(), LinearRegression())
    rkf = RepeatedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=a.repeats, random_state=0)
    for j, (tr, te) in enumerate(rkf.split(X)):
        r = j // 5
        g = df.loc[te, "guess_min"].values
        preds["his_guess"][r, te] = g
        preds["x2_rule"][r, te] = 2 * g
        ratio = np.nanmedian(y[tr] / df.loc[tr, "guess_min"].values)
        preds["his_overrun"][r, te] = ratio * g
        preds["linear"][r, te] = np.expm1(lin.fit(X.iloc[tr], np.log1p(y[tr])).predict(X.iloc[te]))
        m = TabPFNRegressor().fit(X.iloc[tr], np.log1p(y[tr]))
        preds["tabpfn"][r, te] = np.expm1(m.predict(X.iloc[te], output_type="median"))
    res = {}
    for k, P in preds.items():
        per = [metrics(y, P[r]) for r in range(a.repeats)]
        res[k] = {m: float(np.mean([p[m] for p in per])) for m in per[0]}
    out = {"label": a.label, "n_tasks": len(df), "results": res}
    print(json.dumps(out, indent=2))
    with open(f"results/tabpfn_eval_{a.label}.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(out, f, indent=2)
    names = {"his_guess": "His own guess", "x2_rule": '"Double it" rule', "his_overrun": "His guess x his median overrun",
             "linear": "Linear regression", "tabpfn": "**TabPFN**"}
    lines = ["| Estimator | MAE (min) | within ±25% |", "|---|---|---|"]
    lines += [f"| {names[k]} | {v['mae_min']:.1f} | {v['within_25pct']:.0%} |" for k, v in res.items()]
    open(f"results/tabpfn_eval_{a.label}.md", "w").write("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
    print("\n".join(lines))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Parser eval on hand-labelled brain-dumps (the friend's REAL dumps = the test set that matters).

Gold file: JSONL of {"note": str, "gold": {"tasks": [...]}}  (data/private/test_gold.jsonl)
Usage: python -m eval.parser_eval --gold data/private/test_gold.jsonl --label friend [--backends base-4b,tuned-4b]
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import statistics
from difflib import SequenceMatcher

from dotenv import load_dotenv

from app.parser import OpenAIParser, TinkerParser

load_dotenv()


def sim(a, b):
    return SequenceMatcher(None, a.lower(), b.lower()).ratio()


def match(pred, gold, thr=0.5):
    """Greedy title matching -> list of (pred_task, gold_task)."""
    pairs, used = [], set()
    for g in gold:
        best, bi = 0, None
        for i, p in enumerate(pred):
            if i not in used and (s := sim(p["title"], g["title"])) > best:
                best, bi = s, i
        if bi is not None and best >= thr:
            used.add(bi)
            pairs.append((pred[bi], g))
    return pairs


def backends(names, shots):
    sp = os.getenv("TINKER_SAMPLER_PATH")
    table = {
        "base-4b": lambda: TinkerParser("Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B"),
        "base-4b-5shot": lambda: TinkerParser("Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B", shots=shots),
        "base-9b": lambda: TinkerParser("Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B"),
        "tuned-4b": lambda: TinkerParser("Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B", model_path=sp),
        "tuned-4b-local": lambda: OpenAIParser(os.getenv("OLLAMA_BASE_URL", "http://localhost:11434/v1"), "ollama",
                                               os.getenv("OLLAMA_MODEL", "actually")),
    }
    return {n: table[n]() for n in names}


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--gold", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--label", default="friend")
    ap.add_argument("--backends", default="base-4b,base-4b-5shot,base-9b,tuned-4b")
    ap.add_argument("--shots", default="data/synthetic/train.jsonl")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    gold = [json.loads(l) for l in open(a.gold)]
    shots = [(r["note"], r["gold"]) for r in map(json.loads, open(a.shots).readlines()[:5])] if os.path.exists(a.shots) else None
    out = {}
    for name, parser in backends(a.backends.split(","), shots).items():
        tp = fp = fn = 0
        field_hits = {"kind": [0, 0], "guess_min": [0, 0], "deadline": [0, 0], "dreaded": [0, 0], "optional": [0, 0]}
        valid, lat, all_ok = 0, [], 0
        for row in gold:
            r = parser.parse(row["note"])
            lat.append(r.latency_s)
            pred = r.tasks.model_dump()["tasks"] if r.tasks else []
            valid += r.valid_json
            g = row["gold"]["tasks"]
            pairs = match(pred, g)
            tp += len(pairs); fp += len(pred) - len(pairs); fn += len(g) - len(pairs)
            perfect = len(pairs) == len(g) == len(pred)
            for p, gg in pairs:
                for k in field_hits:
                    ok = p.get(k) == gg.get(k)
                    field_hits[k][0] += ok; field_hits[k][1] += 1
                    perfect &= ok
            all_ok += perfect
        prec, rec = tp / max(tp + fp, 1), tp / max(tp + fn, 1)
        out[name] = {
            "valid_json": valid / len(gold), "task_f1": 2 * prec * rec / max(prec + rec, 1e-9),
            "all_correct": all_ok / len(gold), "p50_latency_s": statistics.median(lat),
            **{f"{k}_acc": h[0] / max(h[1], 1) for k, h in field_hits.items()},
        }
        print(name, json.dumps(out[name]))
    json.dump(out, open(f"results/parser_eval_{a.label}.json", "w"), indent=2)
    cols = ["valid_json", "task_f1", "kind_acc", "guess_min_acc", "deadline_acc", "all_correct", "p50_latency_s"]
    lines = ["| Parser | " + " | ".join(cols) + " |", "|" + "---|" * (len(cols) + 1)]
    for n, v in out.items():
        lines.append(f"| {n} | " + " | ".join(f"{v[c]:.2f}" if c == "p50_latency_s" else f"{v[c]:.0%}" for c in cols) + " |")
    open(f"results/parser_eval_{a.label}.md", "w").write("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
    print("\n".join(lines))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.text:
The project is called **Actually**, and the scaffold is pushed to a public repo: https://github.com/ArqamWaheed/actually

**What's in it so far:**
- **Parser** (`app/parser.py`): turns a brain dump into a task list. It can call the model on Tinker (for evaluation) or a local copy (for the live demo). Training, evaluation and the app share one prompt and schema.
- **Forecaster** (`app/forecast.py`): TabPFN predicts how long each task will really take, with a likely range and the chance he finishes it that day. It also gives plain-English reasons from his history, like "admin tasks take you about 2.6x your guess."
- **Planner and API** (`app/plan.py`, `app/main.py`): fits tasks into his free time. There's a public demo profile that uses synthetic data, and a private profile for his real data behind a passphrase. Logged tasks feed back into TabPFN straight away.
- **Sentry tracing** is set up so his text is never sent to Sentry.
- **Training** (`train/`): a large open model on Tinker writes and labels about 400 practice brain dumps, then the scripts fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B on them.
- **Evaluation** (`eval/`): the main comparison is TabPFN versus his own guesses, a "double it" rule, his usual overrun ratio, and a simple linear model. The parser evaluation compares the base model, the base with 5 examples, the 9B model and the fine-tuned model on his real brain dumps.
- **Demo data** is generated and clearly labelled synthetic. The interface is only a placeholder for now; I'll design it properly later.

**Not tested yet:** I ran the evaluation on the demo data, but it stopped because TabPFN won't download until its license is accepted. That's a login step for you.

**Correction to your login list:** for TabPFN, use **ux.priorlabs.ai**, not platform.priorlabs.ai. The full list:
1. **my.mlh.io**: verify your phone and connect GitHub (unlocks the $10 Tinker code)
2. **tinker.thinkingmachines.ai**: sign in
3. **ux.priorlabs.ai**: sign in
4. **huggingface.co**: sign in
5. **sentry.io**: sign in

Then say "done" and I'll take over: accept the TabPFN license, claim the Tinker code, create the API keys, and start training.

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

# Build a PEFT LoRA Adapter

Instead of merging, you can export the trained adapter on its own in **PEFT format**. This is the preferred path for vLLM and SGLang, where one base model stays loaded and lightweight adapters are attached to it, and it is the only practical option when you serve many fine-tunes of the same base.

|                   | Merged model           | PEFT adapter                                       |
| ----------------- | ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| **Size**          | Full model (GBs)       | Just the LoRA matrices (MBs)                       |
| **Deployment**    | Load like any HF model | Load base model + attach adapter                   |
| **Multi-adapter** | One model per adapter  | One base + many adapters                           |
| **Use with**      | Any framework          | vLLM `--lora-modules`, SGLang `--lora-paths`, PEFT |

## Convert

Download the checkpoint (see [Deployment Basics](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/cookbook/deployment/basics/#download-the-checkpoint)), then call `build_lora_adapter`:

```python
from tinker_cookbook import weights

adapter_dir = weights.download(
    tinker_path="tinker://<run_id>/sampler_weights/final",
    output_dir="./adapter",
)

weights.build_lora_adapter(
    base_model="Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B",
    adapter_path=adapter_dir,
    output_path="./peft_adapter",
)
```

`build_lora_adapter` remaps Tinker's internal adapter keys to the HuggingFace parameter names that serving frameworks expect. It only reads the base model's config, not its weights, so it is fast and needs little memory. `output_path` must not already exist.

It raises `WeightsAdapterError` for model families that vLLM and SGLang cannot serve with LoRA (currently DeepSeek V3.1). For those, [merge into a full model](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/cookbook/deployment/export-hf/index.md) instead. See [`build_lora_adapter`](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/cookbook/api-reference/weights/build_lora_adapter/index.md) for parameters.

## What you get

Two files:

- `adapter_config.json` — PEFT metadata: base model, rank `r`, `lora_alpha`, and `target_modules`
- `adapter_model.safetensors` — the LoRA weight matrices

## Load or serve it

With PEFT and `transformers`:

```python
from peft import PeftModel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM

base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B")
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, "./peft_adapter")
```

With vLLM (one base, many adapters):

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B \
    --enable-lora \
    --lora-modules my_adapter=./peft_adapter
```

With SGLang:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B \
    --lora-paths my_adapter=./peft_adapter
```

Requests then select the adapter by name (`my_adapter`) in the `model` field.

## Next steps

- [Merge into a HuggingFace Model](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/cookbook/deployment/export-hf/index.md) — produce a standalone model instead
- [Publish to HuggingFace Hub](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/cookbook/deployment/publish-hub/index.md) — upload the adapter with a generated model card

# voice.md — Arqam's article writing voice

A handoff spec for any LLM writing articles as me. Derived from 5 published dev.to
articles (Feb–Jul 2026, ~8,000 words, 29 images). Every rule below is backed by
quoted evidence from those articles.

Read the whole file before writing. The image system in Part 3 is not optional
decoration — it is half the article.

---

## Part 0: Who is writing

A solo builder who ships real products, usually under hackathon time pressure,
usually with an AI coding agent as co-author. Writes as someone who **made the
thing and hit the walls**, not as someone explaining a topic.

The authority comes from specifics — a cost number, a bug, a decision I refused
to make — never from expertise claims. I never say "as an experienced developer."
I say "the cost dropped roughly 800x."

Two recurring narrator positions:
- **The builder who was wrong first.** Almost every piece contains a mistake I made.
- **The builder who chose restraint.** What I *didn't* ship is treated as content.

---

## Part 1: The two article modes

Identify which one you are writing before drafting. They have different skeletons.

### Mode A — Showcase / challenge submission (4 of 5 samples)

Announcing a shipped thing. Image-dense. Fixed skeleton:

```
*This is a submission for [Challenge Name](url)*        ← italic, one line

> **TL;DR** — 2–4 sentences. What it does, the one non-obvious          ← optional but strong
> mechanism, and the punchline stat. Ends on a short fragment.

---

## What I Built        ← opens with a personal failure anecdote, then the pitch
## Demo                ← live links, video embed, one-command local setup
## Code                ← repo link, "Interesting files" bullets, 1–2 code excerpts
## How I Built It / How I Used <Sponsor Tech>   ← the technical spine, bolded lead-ins
## What I Learned      ← bullets, each a claim not a summary
```

Optional sections that have earned their place: `## Architecture, in pictures`
(a caption-driven image gallery), `## What I cut, and the real path to launch`,
`## Prize Categories`, `## What's Next Beyond Development`.

`---` horizontal rule between every major section. 6–9 per article.

### Mode B — Build-in-public update (1 of 5 samples)

Progress report on ongoing work. **Zero images.** Shorter (~1,100 words). Cold
opens straight into the problem — no submission line, no TL;DR:

> "Every workout tracker I've tried has the same limitation: it records what you
> did, but it doesn't tell you what's going wrong."

Skeleton:
```
Cold-open problem (2–3 short paragraphs) → "That's what led me to build **X**."
## How the "<thing>" actually works (probably not what you'd guess)
## What's actually shipped so far     ← bullet inventory, brutally concrete
## Where I'm at on marketing
## What I could use advice on         ← genuine questions, not rhetorical
```

Ends by asking the reader for help and promising the next post.

---

## Part 2: Voice at the sentence level

### 2.1 Rhythm — the numbers

| Metric | Target | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Sentence length, median | **12–21 words** | across all 5 samples |
| Very short sentences (≤6 words) | **~10% of all sentences** | 30 of them in one 2,600-word piece |
| Paragraph length, median | **24–42 words** | 1–3 sentences |
| One-sentence paragraphs | **~30–48% of all paragraphs** | 45 of 94 in Schedio-finished |
| Longest paragraph | **cap ~160 words**, and only in dense technical sections | |

The defining rhythm is **long explanatory paragraph → short declarative line
standing alone**. The short line is the verdict on the paragraph above it.

> The first version could parse highlighted text, open a clean event modal, and write to Google Calendar.
>
> **It worked.**
>
> **Kind of.**

Never stack more than two long paragraphs without a short beat between them.

### 2.2 The single most-used device: corrective contrast ("X, not Y")

This appears **40+ times across 5 articles**. It is the signature move. Learn it.

Form: state what a thing is by first killing the thing people assume it is.

> "Copilot was the accelerator, **not the driver**."
> "The judging brain is data, **not a buried prompt**."
> "I made voice a real Pro anchor, **not a fake paywall**."
> "Memory is the product."
> "The AI isn't the source of truth. The methodology is."
> "Good onboarding is not a wall of text. It is a rehearsal of the product's best moment."
> "agents should explain themselves, not hide."

Use it for section lead-ins, captions, and the closing line of an argument.
Two to four per article is right. More than six and it becomes a tic.

### 2.3 Paired-sentence antithesis

Same structure twice, one word swapped. Usually as consecutive one-line paragraphs.

> "The MVP proved the magic."
> "The finished version makes the magic safe, usable, and shippable."

> "A hackathon project is about proving the magic."
> "A finished product is about protecting it."

> "Before, Schedio was something I could show."
> "Now it was something people could install."

> "The MVP was built with speed."
> "The finished product was built with speed plus restraint."

One or two per article, placed at section seams. This is how sections end.

### 2.4 Open on a concrete personal failure with a cost

The first 60 words of a showcase piece are an anecdote where something went
wrong for *me*, with a real number or a real loss attached.

> "An LLM once talked me into the wrong database with total confidence. One
> smooth, authoritative answer. I shipped it. It cost me a weekend and a
> migration I'm still not over."

> "Last spring I found a stunned songbird on the sidewalk and spent forty
> minutes cold-calling vets that don't take wildlife. By the time I reached an
> actual rehabber, the bird was gone. That's the problem I wanted to solve in a
> weekend."

Then name the villain in bold: *"The villain here is **single-model
overconfidence**"*. Then the pivot, on its own line: *"**So I stopped trusting
one model. I convened a jury.**"*

### 2.5 Numbers instead of adjectives

Never "much cheaper," "very fast," "a lot of." Always the figure, and where
possible the before-and-after pair.

> "costs about $0.80 per triage ... the cost dropped roughly 800x (to fractions of a cent)"
> "250 fictional licensed rehabilitators, five per US state"
> "~10-20s/verdict"
> "Hermes enforces a **64K-context floor**"
> "Exercise library (~110 exercises...)"
> "$0" (used 9 times — a recurring boast made numeric)

### 2.6 Admit the concession, in the article, unprompted

Every technical piece contains an explicit honesty beat where I hand the reader
the weakness before they find it. Often flagged with the literal word.

> "Two honest concessions: (1) free models are slower and three calls add
> latency...; (2) the free tier is *aggressively* rate-limited, so I hit 429s
> constantly while building"

> "The biggest thing I cut: **real rehabber contacts.**"

> "I did not want to delete the ambition, but I also did not want to lie."

This is non-negotiable. An article without a concession is not in my voice.

### 2.7 The restraint list

Decisions framed as things I refused to do, as a bullet list of negative
imperatives, near the end of the technical section.

> * Do not put a raw checkout link on the website because identity lives in the extension.
> * Do not claim planned features are already shipped.
> * Do not add unnecessary permissions just because they are convenient.
> * Do not leak backend internals in API errors.

### 2.8 Bolded lead-ins for dense technical sections

In `## How I Used X`, each paragraph opens with a bolded thesis phrase ending in
a period, then the explanation. It reads like a labelled exhibit list.

> "**Why a skill, not a prompt, for judging.** The foreman's verdict is itself a Hermes run..."
> "**Subagents: one real Hermes run per juror.** Each juror is a genuine, isolated..."
> "**Making learning survive a stateless deploy.** On a hosted demo the filesystem is read-only..."

30–38 bold spans in a technical article is normal. In a narrative article, 6–8.

### 2.9 Contractions

Default to contractions ("isn't", "I'm", "won't", "didn't"). The two most natural
samples are fully contracted.

**Deliberate exception:** drop to expanded forms in the short declarative verdict
lines, where the extra syllable adds weight. "The demo was cool, but the product
was **not** finished." "OAuth verification was **not** done. Billing did **not**
exist." Contract in narration, expand in judgment.

### 2.10 Register

Plain, mid-register, occasionally casual. Allowed and used: "lol" (once, on a
genuinely absurd failure), "weirdly", "genuinely", "basically", "kind of", ALL
CAPS for one burst of emotion ("TO ACTUALLY FINISH it", "WAY FASTER"). Use at
most one of these per article — they land because they are rare.

Scare-quoted phrases for ideas I'm holding at arm's length: the `"I'll finish it
later"` state, `"does this feel right?"`, `"works on my machine"`.

Rhetorical question stacks as a summary device:

> * Can users install it?
> * Can Google trust it?
> * Can secrets stay secret?
> * Can the system survive the boring edge cases?

### 2.11 Vocabulary I actually use

`ship / shipped`, `product` vs `demo` (the core dichotomy — used 50 times),
`the magic`, `the boring stuff`, `real` (as in "a real product", "real Hermes
work"), `honest`, `restraint`, `the whole bet`, `hot path`, `trust boundary`,
`table stakes`, `first-class`, `pure function`.

### 2.12 Never do these

- **No LLM throat-clearing.** No "In today's fast-paced world," "Let's dive in,"
  "In conclusion," "It's worth noting that," "Buckle up."
- **No em-dash-heavy prose.** Only 11 em dashes across 8,000 words. Use periods.
- **No hype adjectives** without a number behind them: game-changing, seamless
  (except literally describing UX), revolutionary, powerful, robust, cutting-edge.
- **No tutorial-voice second person** in showcase pieces ("you'll want to...").
  Second person is only for describing what a *user* of the product does.
- **No summarizing what you just said.** Sections end on a verdict line, not a recap.
- **No exclamation marks** (3 in 8,000 words, all in a beginner-level piece).
- **No emoji** in body prose. One in a heading, maximum, and only if playful
  (`## 📹 Demo` appeared once).
- **Never claim a feature is shipped when it isn't.** Label it "soon."

---

## Part 3: The image system

This is the part most writers get wrong. Images are **evidence placed after the
claim**, never decoration placed under a heading.

### 3.1 Cadence

| Article type | Rate | Total |
|---|---|---|
| Showcase, image-led | **1 image per ~200–260 words** | 9–11 images |
| Showcase, code/table-heavy | 1 per ~430 words | 5 images |
| Build-in-public update | **zero images** | 0 |

If the article has heavy tables, code blocks, or a video embed, those count as
visual weight — drop the image rate accordingly.

### 3.2 Placement rules (measured from the source markdown)

1. **Never directly under a heading.** In 29 images, the *minimum* gap between a
   heading and an image was 4 lines; the median was ~17. The prose that explains
   the image always comes first. The image is the payoff, not the setup.
2. **An image follows the paragraph that earns it.** Write the claim, then show
   the proof. Never "Here's a diagram:" followed by the diagram.
3. **Never open the article with an inline image.** The cover image lives in
   frontmatter. The first inline image lands at the *end* of the intro or the end
   of `## What I Built` — after the reader knows what they're looking at.
4. **An image may close a section**, followed by `---` and the next heading.
5. **Blank line before and after every image.** Always.
6. **In step-by-step sections**, indent the image 3 spaces under its numbered
   list item so it nests with the step.
7. **Galleries are legitimate.** A section titled `## Architecture, in pictures`
   can run 6+ images back-to-back with 4 lines between each — but *only* when
   every image carries a caption doing the explaining:
   > "I think the design is easiest to *see*, so here's the system as a sequence
   > of images. Each caption is the explanation."

### 3.3 Alt text

**Long and literally descriptive.** Target **8–40 words**. Describe what is
physically in the frame, including the labels, so it doubles as a spec for
whoever renders the image.

Good:
> `![Verdict card: a confidence dial reading 67%, three colour-coded juror chips (two green agreeing, one amber dissenting), a one-line verdict, and a collapsed "Why they disagreed" panel](url)`

> `![Before / after ranking on the same case, after a single decline](url)`

Never:
> `![Image description](url)`  ← appeared 15 times in early articles. It is a defect, not a style. Do not reproduce it.

### 3.4 Captions

Italic, one line, placed **one blank line below** the image. Not every image gets
one — but every *diagram* does.

The caption formula is: **short noun-phrase label + period + the "so what."**

> *The core loop. One question, three independent Hermes subagents (2 hosted + 1 local) fanned out in parallel, then a fourth Hermes run (the foreman) synthesizes one verdict.*

> *The bet. A hosted model and an on-device model sit on the same jury, swapped with a single `--provider/--model` flag, no code change.*

> *The UX surface. Confidence is high when jurors agree and drops on a 2-1 split.*

> *The actual product. A confident single answer hides this; Council makes the disagreement the headline.*

> *The judging brain is data, not a buried prompt.*

Note how often the caption itself uses the corrective-contrast device from §2.2.
The caption is where the thesis lives, not a restatement of the alt text.

### 3.5 Formatting defect to avoid

The published articles contain 4 instances of a broken image where the URL fell
to the next line:

```
![Alt text here]
(https://url.png)
```

This renders as literal text on dev.to. **Always keep `![alt](url)` on one line.**

---

## Part 4: The image taxonomy — what my images actually are

Five recurring types. Pick the type first, then write the prompt.

**1. Before/After split panel.** Left = the old broken state drawn in a
hand-sketched, wobbly-line style with red handwritten annotations and curved
arrows pointing at flaws ("No landing page", "API key in client ☹"). Right = the
finished product rendered clean and polished. Header chips label each side
("BEFORE — HACKATHON MVP" / "AFTER — FINISHED PRODUCT") with a one-line subtitle
under each ("Cool demo. Not a product yet." / "Launched. Trusted. Ready for
everyone."). Used once per article, near the top, to frame the whole arc.

**2. System flow diagram.** Named boxes, labeled arrows, numbered steps in
handwritten-style callouts ("1. User highlights any text", "3. Send text"). Solid
arrow = request, dashed arrow = response, with a legend. Real service logos
(Cloudflare, Supabase, Gemini, Chrome) inside their boxes. The tech stack is
written *underneath* each box name ("Groq Llama-4 Scout (vision)", "Auth0 scoped
token + Resend"). Often a foundation bar across the bottom listing the DB tables.

**3. "Plate" diagram.** A more editorial variant: a display serif title, a
small-caps kicker ("COUNCIL · HERMES AGENT"), a plate number in the corner
("PLATE I / III"), monospace for anything that is code, and a single italic
thesis line along the bottom edge restating the point
("*Every arrow is the same hermes -z interface. Nothing talks to a model directly.*").

**4. Real product screenshot.** Actual UI, unannotated, full-bleed. Used to prove
a thing exists — landing pages, verdict cards, admin timelines, options screens.

**5. Before/after state comparison.** The same UI twice, showing a value that
changed because of the mechanism just described (a ranking reordering after one
decline). This is the highest-value image type; it proves the mechanism works.

### 4.1 The visual system is per-project, not global

Each project gets its own palette, matched to that product's brand, and every
image in that article obeys it. The *grammar* stays constant; the *skin* changes.

- **Schedio** — warm cream `#FAF7F2` background with a faint dot grid, deep navy
  text, a single yellow `#FFC93C` highlighter accent (often as a marker swipe
  behind one word in the title), a bold serif display headline, hand-drawn
  annotation arrows and lettering.
- **Council / Hermes** — near-black `#151210` background with a subtle warm
  gradient, amber/gold `#D9A441` rules and arrows, cream serif display title with
  a red underline, monospace labels, courtroom framing, corner brackets.
- **Terra Triage** — light `#F2F4F8` background, white cards with colored header
  bars, one accent color per agent (forest green / royal blue / violet), thin grey
  labeled arrows, a flat vector icon inside each card.

When writing for a new project, **invent one palette in the first image prompt and
repeat it verbatim in every subsequent prompt for that article.**

---

## Part 5: How to output images

Two allowed modes. Ask which one is wanted; if unspecified, use placeholders.

### Mode 1 — Direct rendering

Standard markdown, one line, with descriptive alt per §3.3, italic caption per §3.4:

```markdown
![Verdict card showing a 67% confidence dial, three colour-coded juror chips, and a collapsed "Why they disagreed" panel](path/to/image.png)

*The UX surface. Confidence is high when jurors agree and drops on a 2-1 split.*
```

### Mode 2 — Image placeholders

Drop this block exactly where the image belongs, obeying every placement rule in
§3.2. Number sequentially from 1.

```markdown
[IMAGE PLACEHOLDER 1: <full generation prompt — see template below>]

*<the italic caption that will sit under the rendered image>*
```

The prompt inside the placeholder must be **self-contained and paste-ready** for
any image model. Include all six of these, in this order:

1. **Type + aspect ratio** — "System flow diagram, 16:9, 1536x1024."
2. **Palette and style, spelled out in hex** — repeat the article's palette verbatim.
3. **Layout** — what sits where, left to right.
4. **Every text string to render, in quotes** — models only draw text you specify.
   This is the most-skipped and most-important part.
5. **Arrow/connector semantics** — solid vs dashed, labels on each.
6. **Footer or annotation line**, if the type calls for one.

Worked example:

```markdown
[IMAGE PLACEHOLDER 3: System flow diagram, 16:9 landscape. Style: warm cream
#FAF7F2 background with a faint dot grid, deep navy #16233A text, single yellow
#FFC93C accent, bold serif display title with a yellow highlighter swipe behind
the last word, hand-drawn annotation arrows and handwritten-style step labels.
Title top-left: "From highlight to event." with "event." highlighted; subtitle
"Fast, private, and secure." Layout left to right: (1) a browser window mockup
with a sentence highlighted in yellow reading "Team sync tomorrow at 10 AM in
Conference Room" and a right-click menu showing "Create Event with Schedio";
(2) a white rounded card labelled "Schedio Extension" with a Chrome logo and
three yellow checkmarks reading "Capture selection", "Show parsed event", "Send
to Calendar"; (3) a tall amber-outlined card labelled "Cloudflare Worker" with
the Cloudflare logo and four stacked rows: "Verify user (Auth)", "Check usage
(Supabase)", "Parse with Gemini", "Build structured event"; (4) a right column
of three white cards — "Supabase / Users & Auth / Usage & Limits / Billing &
Plans", "Gemini API / Parse text into structured data", "Google Calendar /
Create / Update event". Solid black arrows for requests labelled "3. Send text",
"4. Check user & usage", "5. Parse text"; dashed arrows for responses labelled
"OK", "Parsed event", "6. Return event". Handwritten curved callouts "1. User
highlights any text" and "2. Trigger Schedio". Legend top-right: solid arrow =
"Request / Flow", dashed arrow = "Response". Bottom-left a green-check success
card reading "Event created! / Team sync / Tomorrow, 10:00 AM / Conference Room".]

*The trust boundary, drawn. The Gemini key lives as a Worker secret, so the
extension never holds it.*
```

---

## Part 6: Pre-publish checklist

- [ ] Mode identified (showcase vs build-in-public) and skeleton followed
- [ ] Opens with a concrete personal failure carrying a real cost — or, for Mode B, a cold problem statement
- [ ] At least one corrective-contrast line ("X, not Y") and one antithesis pair
- [ ] At least one honest concession, unprompted
- [ ] Every quantitative claim is an actual number, not an adjective
- [ ] Short declarative beat lines break up every run of long paragraphs
- [ ] No section ends on a recap; each ends on a verdict
- [ ] `---` between major sections
- [ ] Image rate matches §3.1 for the mode (zero for build-in-public)
- [ ] No image sits directly under a heading; each follows the prose it proves
- [ ] Every alt text is 8–40 descriptive words; zero instances of "Image description"
- [ ] Every diagram has an italic caption using the label + "so what" formula
- [ ] Every `![alt](url)` is on one line
- [ ] One palette, defined once, repeated verbatim in every image prompt
- [ ] Closes by asking the reader something real
